source.title: Flat Posterior Does Matter For Bayesian Transfer Learning
source.authors: Sung-Jun Lim; Jeyoon Yeom; Sooyon Kim; Hoyoon Byun; Jinho Kang; Yohan Jung; Jiyoung Jung; Kyungwoo Song

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and appendix; the title in the text differs slightly from the catalog title. No relevant sections appear cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether posterior flatness and a flatness-seeking training objective relate to Bayesian model averaging generalization, using posterior Hessian eigenvalues and predictive metrics rather than the claim versions’ original interventions.
record.gate_note: The study tests properties of Bayesian posterior flatness and reports held-out classification metrics, but does not test memorization of random labels, width beyond interpolation, CNN versus fully connected generalization, optimizer or batch-size generalization gaps as stated in V4–V5, dropout, or removal of memorized examples. Test-set results and correlations with test metrics do not measure the training–test gap required by V7.
record.test_reason: The study investigates a related flatness–generalization question, but none of V1–V8. Its closest results to V7 correlate unscaled Hessian eigenvalues with held-out error, ECE, and NLL; they do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, training–test gaps, or rankings against norm and margin measures. The theoretical bound also concerns a different sharpness measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors conclude that approximate Bayesian inference can produce insufficiently flat posteriors, limiting BMA performance, and that FP-BMA improves predictive performance and transfer robustness by seeking flatter posteriors. Their conclusion does not establish that BMA cannot improve generalization without flat samples; they acknowledge strong theoretical assumptions and incomplete MCMC coverage.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies Bayesian posterior flatness and Bayesian model averaging, with a new FP-BMA objective and Hessian-eigenvalue analysis. It does not reproduce the interventions or measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported flatness–metric correlation holds across Constant, Cosine Decay, and SWAG learning-rate schedulers and across CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; appendix text says the correlations are strong regardless of scheduler and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 30 sampled SWAG models per setting, maximal Hessian eigenvalues correlate strongly with held-out classification error, ECE, and NLL on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 across three learning-rate schedulers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Hessian sharpness is associated with predictive performance among sampled Bayesian models in these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: FP-BMA improves predictive performance and reaches predictive convergence with fewer posterior samples than the compared SGD-trained Bayesian methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicitly seeking flat posteriors can improve Bayesian model averaging performance and sample efficiency in the tested CIFAR10 settings.

fits_no_version.finding: FP-BMA has the lowest largest Hessian eigenvalue and eigenvalue ratio among Table 5 methods on ResNet18 CIFAR10 10-shot.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FP-BMA produces lower measured posterior Hessian sharpness than the tested comparison methods.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: The paper's empirical flatness analysis uses Hessian eigenvalues, not magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or an explicit train–test gap. Correlation coefficients are not supplied in the text. The conclusion notes strong assumptions in the theoretical insights and that empirical evaluation does not cover the full spectrum of MCMC algorithms.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible version-mapped results were reported. Rows were retained for relevant findings about posterior flatness and predictive metrics, but these do not measure the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting compared with natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy under the same training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; the Bayesian and sharpness-aware method comparisons do not isolate this question.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove those effects.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size, dropout strength, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness tracking training–test gaps among similarly fitted networks, including rankings against norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. The posterior-flatness bound in Section 3.1 and Appendix B.1 does not establish V7's empirical magnitude-aware sharpness ranking. All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions, without disputing the reported related findings.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and local-connectivity effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance under limited tuning.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of training–test gaps; the paper measures Hessian eigenvalues and test metrics, not magnitude-aware sharpness or gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test-accuracy effects.

rows.check: This is the proposed method's performance comparison, not an eligible claim-version result. It also combines classification error, ECE, NLL, and sample-count convergence in one row.
